key_insight: Visual language models (VLMs) match humans on high-level object recognition but exhibit widespread deficits on standardized low- and mid-level visual neuropsychological tests, revealing systematic perceptual weaknesses beneath their apparent competence.
problem_solved: The paper evaluates whether current VLMs truly replicate human visual abilities across the full hierarchy of perception, rather than just high-level recognition, by applying standardized neuropsychological assessments.
method: Assembled a battery of standardized neuropsychological visual tests that probe low-level (e.g., contrast, spatial resolution), mid-level (e.g., grouping, contour integration), and high-level (object recognition) abilities.
Presented controlled stimuli to multiple state-of-the-art VLMs via task-appropriate prompts and scoring rules, then measured performance against human norms and statistical baselines.
Analyzed patterns of failure across tasks to identify systematic deficits and dissociations between high-level success and low-/mid-level impairments.
impact: Highlights a critical gap in VLM perceptual competence that affects robustness, generalization, and safety-sensitive applications; encourages researchers to benchmark models across hierarchical visual functions and to design architectures or training that explicitly target low- and mid-level vision.
visual_elements: Bar chart comparing human vs VLM performance across low-, mid-, and high-level test groups (clear deficit bars for low/mid).
Example stimulus panels showing specific VLM failure modes (e.g., poor contour integration, contrast insensitivity) alongside correct human responses.
Radar/spider plot of perceptual ability profile for humans vs representative VLMs to visualize strengths and weaknesses.
Pipeline diagram: standardized tests → VLM prompting → scoring → human-norm comparison (to show experimental flow).
paper_title: Visual language models show widespread visual deficits on neuropsychological tests
